groups.passage:
Water Refill Stations at a Sports Centre

A sports centre introduced three water refill stations after staff noticed that its rubbish bins were often full of disposable bottles. The centre placed two stations near the changing rooms and one beside the indoor courts. Visitors could continue to buy drinks at the reception desk, but they were encouraged to bring reusable bottles.

During the first month, staff recorded how often each station was used. The machine near the courts proved especially popular, and queues sometimes formed between classes. The manager moved a less frequently used station from a changing-room corridor to the entrance of the courts. Staff also added clear signs explaining where visitors could refill bottles.

After three months, the centre reported a reduction in the number of disposable bottles collected from its bins. The manager decided to keep monitoring water use and maintenance costs before ordering any additional machines. She also invited visitors to report problems through a short online form.

options.text: Its reception desk had stopped selling drinks.
The courts needed additional changing rooms.
Visitors had complained about the opening hours.
Its bins frequently contained many disposable bottles.

Why did the manager relocate one station?

options.text: To remove a machine that could not be repaired.

To provide another refill point near the busy courts.

options.text: Continue checking water consumption and maintenance expenses.

groups.passage:
A Museum Collection Visitors Can Touch

For many years, a small local museum displayed most of its historical objects behind glass. This protected fragile items, but it also limited how visitors could explore their shapes and textures. A teacher working with students who had limited vision asked the museum whether some objects could be experienced through touch.

The museum began by selecting five objects that illustrated everyday life in the past. A craft worker made durable replicas using materials that reproduced important features of the originals. The replicas included a wooden comb, a ceramic cup and a small weaving tool. Staff placed short audio descriptions next to the objects and invited students to test the display.

Feedback revealed that even a carefully made replica needed a clear explanation. Students wanted to know which parts reflected the original accurately and which parts had been modified for safety or durability. In response, museum staff revised the descriptions and provided a brief explanation of the production process.

The new display was later opened to all visitors. Families reported that handling the replicas encouraged children to ask questions about how the original objects were used. Museum staff continued to protect the historical collection while using the replicas to offer a different form of learning. They also began considering which future exhibitions might benefit from a similar approach.

questions.question_text: What limitation of the original display is mentioned in paragraph 1?

options.text: Visitors could not readily explore objects through touch.
The display included no objects from everyday life.
Visitors were not allowed to enter with teachers.
The museum had difficulty keeping its doors open.

questions.question_text: What was the craft worker asked to make?

options.text: Glass cases with stronger locks for the collection.
New objects unrelated to the museum's historical collection.
Robust copies that retained key features of the historical objects.
Audio recordings of traditional craft techniques.

questions.question_text: What does "the originals" in paragraph 2 refer to?

options.text: The audio descriptions played for the students.
The historical objects selected for replication.
The materials supplied by the craft worker.
The first visitors to test the display.

questions.question_text: What did the students' feedback lead the museum to change?

options.text: The number of historical objects stored behind glass.
The materials used in every object in the original collection.
The museum's policy on admitting school groups.
The information explaining the replicas and how they were produced.

questions.question_text: What can be inferred from the families' reports?

options.text: Children preferred to take original objects home.
The tactile display also supported learning for children beyond the original target group.
Families wanted all audio descriptions to be removed.
The museum could no longer protect its historical collection.

questions.question_text: Which statement best expresses the main message of the article?

options.text: Historical collections are most valuable when every item can be handled freely.
Audio descriptions are unnecessary whenever replicas are available.
Museums should replace all historical collections with replicas.
Well-explained replicas can improve access and learning while originals remain protected.

groups.instructions: Read the essay and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
Keeping Community Stories Accessible

When a neighbourhood history group began collecting interviews with long-term residents, its members assumed that the most difficult task would be persuading people to share their memories. Many residents, however, were happy to participate. The harder question was how to keep their stories accessible for future readers without losing the context in which they had been told.

The group's first recordings were stored on a single computer. Volunteers gave them file names based on the date of each interview and wrote brief notes about the speakers. When a volunteer tried to find every account of an old market, she discovered that identifying relevant recordings required listening to large sections of audio. Dates helped organise the files, but they revealed little about the subjects discussed.

The group then introduced a simple catalogue. Each entry included a list of topics, the approximate location of events and a description of the speaker's connection to them. Volunteers were careful to distinguish between information provided by the interviewee and details added later by researchers. If two residents remembered the same event differently, both accounts were retained, together with notes indicating the differences. The group believed that such disagreements could themselves be valuable historical evidence.

Another concern involved long-term storage. The members arranged to keep copies in two separate locations and chose widely supported audio formats. They also set a reminder to check the files periodically. They recognised that storing a digital file today did not guarantee that it would remain readable in twenty years. Equipment, software and file formats could all change.

Finally, the group discussed who should have access to the interviews. Some speakers were comfortable with public access, while others wanted particular sections to be available only to researchers. Rather than applying a single rule, the group recorded each person's choices and attached access instructions to the relevant catalogue entries. Volunteers were required to consult these instructions before sharing material.

The project eventually produced an archive that was easier to search and better prepared for future technological changes. Its members learned that preserving a story requires attention to much more than the recording itself. Information about its content, origin and permitted use can determine whether the story remains both meaningful and responsibly accessible.
